detail:
The Average Stock Shrugged Off the Tech Slide. History Is Split

IWM

Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

For most of this bull market, investors could count on one rule. The biggest stocks lead. When a few tech giants rise, the S&P 500 rises with them. When they fall, the rest of the market falls too. Over the past month, that rule bent. From Oct. 23 to Nov. 24, the regular S&P 500 fund (SPY) lost 5.42%. The equal-weight S&P 500 fund (RSP), which gives each of the 500 companies the same weight, lost only 1.19%. The Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) fund lost 9.41% over the same dates. The average stock fell far less than the giants, after the giants' lead hit a record on Oct. 7. Whether that lasts is the open question.

The Nasdaq-100 fund fell 9.41% in a single month while the average stock lost only 1.19%. A drop like that is easier to sit through when your savings do not hang on a few tech stocks. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.

How the Biggest Stocks Took Over

One simple gauge tracks this rule. Take the value of the equal-weight fund, with dividends reinvested, and divide it by the value of the regular S&P 500 fund on the same day. The ratio falls when the biggest stocks do better than the average one. At the end of 2014 it stood at 0.388. That was its highest year-end reading in data that start in 2003.

Then it slid for a decade. The ratio was 0.328 at the end of 2023, 0.296 at the end of 2024 and 0.280 at the end of 2025. It kept falling this year. On Oct. 7 it reached 0.271, the lowest since the data begin.

What Changed This Year

The ratio turned in early October. From its Oct. 7 low of 0.271, it climbed to 0.298 on Nov. 24. That is above its reading of 0.280 at the end of 2025.

Over the year as a whole, the average stock has also beaten tech. From Dec. 31, 2025 to Nov. 24, the equal-weight fund returned 13.03%, dividends included. The Nasdaq-100 fund returned 4.23%. But the largest S&P 500 names kept their lead over the average stock until early October.

Correlation measures how closely two prices move together, where 1 means in lockstep and 0 means unrelated. The equal-weight fund and the Nasdaq-100 fund have moved less closely day to day this year. Their correlation of daily moves has averaged 0.57 so far in 2026, tied with 2021 for the lowest yearly average in data back to 2015. In 2022 it averaged 0.89. Over the last 63 trading days it was 0.66 as of Nov. 24. So lately the two funds have moved a bit more in step day to day. Over the past month they still moved by very different amounts.

If you look at the performance of growth-oriented exchange-traded funds (ETFs) over the past five years, you'd probably expect to see names like the Invesco QQQ (NASDAQ:QQQ) among the top performers.

But there is another smaller, less well-known ETF that has outperformed the QQQ over the past five years -- the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF (NYSEMKT:SPMO).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

If you had $200 to start investing, this surprisingly adept ETF would be a good place to start -- even better, perhaps, than the QQQ or an S&P 500 ETF.

Businesswoman holding glasses while working on a laptop in a bright modern office.

Image source: Getty Images.

Tracking the top 100 S&P 500 stocks

The Invesco QQQ is one of the largest ETFs in the world with some $448 billion in assets under management. It invests in the Nasdaq 100, which includes the 100 largest stocks in the Nasdaq Composite not including financial stocks.

The Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF is not as widely known as the QQQ, or as big. It only has about $19 billion in assets under management. However, it has returns that are very competitive with the QQQ.

It is also somewhat of a companion ETF to the QQQ because it invests in the roughly 100 stocks in the S&P 500 that have the highest momentum score, via the S&P Momentum index.

The momentum score is calculated by determining the 100 stocks that have the largest percentage change in the stock price over the previous 12 months, excluding the most recent month. There is also an adjustment based on the stock's volatility over that period.

The top three holdings in SPMO are Apple, Micron Technology, and Johnson & Johnson. For comparison, the QQQ's top three holdings are Nvidia, Apple, and Alphabet.

Beating the QQQ over the past five years

Over the past three years, the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF has posted an average annualized return of 26.2% vs. 18.6% for the QQQ over that same stretch. Over the past five years, SPMO has posted a 13.9% average annualized return compared to 10.3% for the QQQ.

The QQQ does have the edge over the past 10 years, with an average annualized return of 18.5% compared to SPMO's 16.8% return. In addition, SPMO beats the S&P 500 over each of the three-, five-, and 10-year periods.

Certainly, the QQQ is a popular choice among investors, but the SPMO should not be overlooked. It has a lower expense ratio at 0.13% compared to 0.18% for the QQQ. It also has performed far better in a down market, mainly because of its momentum qualities. During 2022, when the QQQ dropped 33%, mirroring the Nasdaq 100's decline that year, the SPMO was down just 12% -- which even beat the S&P 500's 19% decline.

Berkshire stock is up 15% year to date (YTD) to $577.76 in afternoon trading. The Class B shares are up 0.1% from the prior close while NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) leads a renewed wave of the AI selloff. The hot reading has all but locked in a December Federal Reserve rate hike, and the AI selloff is hitting tech-heavy indexes hardest, which plays to Berkshire's defensive profile.

Management called such gains "usually meaningless,". So the operating figure gives the cleaner read, with BNSF, Berkshire Hathaway Energy and the manufacturing, service and retailing group all growing.

Anthony Di Pizio, The Motley Fool

Trading disclosure

The Nasdaq-100 is an index of the 100 most valuable companies listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange, excluding banks and financial institutions. The index is highly concentrated, with technology companies alone representing over 60% of its value, which means it has significant exposure to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

Investors have dumped AI stocks over the last month, partly because of the turmoil at semiconductor giant Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA). Founder Jensen Huang left the company on Nov. 12 after his marital infidelity came to light, casting a cloud of uncertainty over the company's future. He was reinstated this past Monday, but I predict his decisions will face more oversight from the board of directors going forward, so he might be far more conservative, especially when it comes to things like investing in other AI companies.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The Invesco QQQ ETF (NASDAQ:QQQ) is an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that mimics the performance of the Nasdaq-100 by holding the same stocks. As of the market close last Friday, it was down 19.8% from its October peak along with the index. It's now mounting a recovery, so could this be the ultimate long-term buying opportunity?

Image source: Getty Images.

Broad exposure to America's greatest technology stocks

Major technological shifts rarely go smoothly, particularly when they have such a significant impact on consumers and businesses. Enterprise software and cloud computing companies experienced plenty of challenges on the road to mass adoption, so the AI industry is likely to face many headwinds.

Fortunately, the Nasdaq-100 index primarily holds the largest, most established companies in the AI space. They include semiconductor suppliers, application developers, cloud providers, and more. The top 10 positions in the Invesco QQQ ETF include a healthy mix of those companies, and they represent 46.1% of the value of its entire portfolio.
